title: Attributing perceived unfairness to another's perspective
description: This latent activates on sentences that articulate how another person might perceive or feel about an action as unfair, particularly framing a conflict in terms of violated expectations of shared or communal resources. It responds to hedged mental-state attributions ('they might feel', 'you're being unfair') that explain the emotional or moral reasoning behind someone's reaction to another's behavior. It is not simply about fairness or conflict in the abstract, nor about the speaker's own feelings of unfairness; it specifically captures the act of modeling and voicing a third party's perceived grievance. Sentences that state fairness violations as objective fact, or that describe unfairness without reference to another's internal perspective, would not activate it.

title: Numbered list markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral or bullet marker that begins an item in an enumerated or numbered list, especially the digit itself (often followed by a period or a bold-markdown asterisk), rather than on the content of the item. It activates strongly on isolated tokens like '4.', '9', '3.', or '2. **' that mark list positions in advice-giving or step-by-step text. It does not activate on the prose sentences that make up the substance of the advice (e.g., recommendations about prioritizing well-being or communication), only on the structural numbering tokens that organize such lists.

title: AITA closing question
description: This latent fires almost exclusively on the literal closing phrase 'AITA?' (often preceded by 'So,'), the stock sign-off used at the end of Reddit 'Am I the Asshole' posts to prompt readers for a verdict. It activates most strongly on the bare interrogative itself, essentially treating it as a fixed formulaic token/phrase rather than responding to surrounding judgment content. The weaker/random activations show it also lights up, to a lesser degree, on related verdict-seeking or moral-judgment language within AITA-style responses (e.g. 'you're not the asshole', 'WIBTA', discussions weighing whether someone was wrong), but these are secondary compared to the sharp peak on the literal 'AITA?' sign-off. It would not activate on general questions, other topic content, or moral reasoning sentences that don't reference the AITA/WIBTA framing or its closing query.

title: Reassuring affirmation to 'you'
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic second-person affirmations of encouragement and self-worth, typically beginning with 'Remember,' 'You are,' or 'You deserve,' that assert the listener's strength, worthiness, or capability (e.g., 'you are strong, capable, and deserving of love and respect,' 'you are not alone'). It activates most strongly on templated, uplifting closing-style statements that combine reassurance ('not alone,' 'will get through this') with affirmations of value ('deserving of love/respect,' 'worthy,' 'enough'), often stacked in a formulaic list structure. It does not activate strongly on advice-giving, analytical, or empathetic-but-descriptive sentences that discuss someone's situation, feelings, or actions in third person or explanatory terms (e.g., 'It's understandable that you feel...' or 'You could argue that...'), even when second-person and supportive in tone, since those lack the direct affirming/reassuring address pattern this latent targets.

title: Empathetic validation and reassurance in interpersonal advice
description: This latent fires on sentences that validate a person's feelings or perspective in an emotionally charged interpersonal situation, typically using phrases like 'it's understandable that...' or absolving statements like 'you're not responsible for...'. These sentences function as supportive, therapeutic-style responses that acknowledge difficult emotions or defend/excuse someone's behavior/choices without necessarily resolving the underlying conflict. It is active on advice-column or counseling-register language offering empathy, reassurance, or reframing of blame. It would not activate on neutral factual statements, direct advice/instructions, or emotionally charged statements that lack this validating/absolving framing (e.g., simply describing a conflict or criticizing someone).

title: Numbered list markers
description: This latent fires on standalone numeral tokens (e.g., '2.', '3.', '4.') that serve as list-item markers, typically beginning a new point in an enumerated list such as reasons, suggestions, or considerations. It activates most strongly on the bare number-plus-period token itself, regardless of the content that follows or precedes it. It also fires, more weakly, on surrounding sentences that are part of such enumerated advice/reasoning lists (e.g., 'Here's why: 1.'), since these co-occur with the numbering pattern. It would not activate on ordinary prose sentences lacking list structure, or on numbers used in non-list contexts like dates, quantities, or measurements.

title: Clarifying follow-up question to user
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic conversational prompts—often from an advice-giving or chatbot persona—that invite the user to elaborate, share more detail, or state their opinion, such as 'What do you think?', 'Can you tell me more about...', or 'Is everything okay?'. It activates most strongly on generic, templated question stems that solicit the interlocutor's feelings, thoughts, or missing context, and also fires (more weakly) on numbered list markers like '2.' or '3.' that likely co-occur with these dialogue turns in structured responses. It does not activate on declarative advice, explanations, or substantive statements that answer or elaborate on a topic rather than prompting the other party to respond—i.e., content-rich reasoning or reassurance sentences are excluded even when thematically similar (e.g., relationship advice paragraphs) unless they end in or consist of a direct solicitation question.

title: List-introducing lead-in phrase
description: This latent fires on the short introductory clause that immediately precedes an enumerated list, such as 'Here are some suggestions:', 'Here's a possible approach:', or 'Here are some tips:', typically followed by a numbered '1.' marker. It activates most strongly on these formulaic transitional phrases themselves, regardless of what the list content will be about (advice, steps, approaches, frameworks, etc.), and is largely insensitive to topic. It does not activate on the actual list items or advice content that follows (e.g., 'Be mindful of...', 'Focus on your own relationships...'), nor on other transitional or discourse-marking sentences that don't specifically announce an upcoming enumerated list, such as general reassurances, empathetic statements, or requests for more information.

title: Suggested activities in listicle form
description: This latent fires on short, list-item recommendations of concrete activities or hobbies (e.g., 'Take a class or workshop', 'Try painting, drawing, or photography', 'Go for a walk or hike'), typically phrased as imperative bullet points offering options for self-improvement, leisure, exercise, or creative pursuits. It activates most strongly on formulaic advice-list entries with bolded headers followed by a colon and a short list of example activities, often in response to prompts about stress relief, hobbies, side income, or self-care. It does not activate on general conversational advice, reflective commentary, interpersonal reasoning, or numbered list markers without concrete activity content (e.g., 'It's important to respect boundaries' or bare enumerators like '5. **'), even when these appear in similarly structured advice-giving text.

title: Empathic acknowledgment opener
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic exclamatory phrases that open a response by validating the user's feelings or situation, especially stock expressions like 'I totally/completely understand!' and 'I totally get it!', often followed by 'your concern(s)/struggle/dilemma.' It also activates, more weakly, on related brief exclamatory framings like 'The eternal dilemma!' or 'A fascinating perspective!' that similarly serve as a punchy affective/acknowledging lead-in. It is most strongly tuned to the exact 'I understand/get it' empathy templates rather than to longer, discursive expressions of sympathy or understanding embedded in fuller sentences (e.g. 'It's completely understandable that you're feeling anxious...'), which activate it much less or not at all. Sentences that merely discuss understanding or empathy as a topic without using this exclamatory acknowledgment phrasing do not trigger it.
